replacement: 4. But someone may say that the senses occasionally mislead us about small objects, or about things too far away to examine closely, yet many other things they report (presentations) cannot manifestly be doubted. For example, that I am in this place, seated by the fire, wearing a winter dressing gown, holding this piece of paper in my hands, and other things of the same kind. But how could I deny that these hands and this body are mine? I would have to count myself among the insane, whose brains are so disordered and clouded by dark bilious vapors that they stubbornly insist they are kings when they are in the greatest poverty, or that they are dressed [in gold] and purple when they have nothing on, or that their head is made of clay, their body of glass, or that they are gourds. But these people are madmen, and I would be no less insane than they if I took such extravagant examples as my guide.

note: Antecedents and consequents recast as causes and effects.
replacement: 10. Some people, indeed, might perhaps be found who would rather deny the existence of so powerful a Being than believe that nothing is certain. But for the present let us not oppose this view, and let us grant that everything said here about a Deity is fable. Still, however it is supposed that I came to be what I am, whether by fate, or chance, or an endless series of antecedents and consequents, or any other means, being deceived and being in error are a certain defect. So it is clear that the probability of my being so imperfect as to be constantly deceived increases exactly as the power of the cause assigned as my origin decreases. To these arguments I have assuredly nothing to reply. I am forced at last to admit that there is nothing among all I formerly believed true that it is impossible to doubt, and this not through thoughtlessness or levity but for cogent and carefully considered reasons. So from now on, if I want to discover anything certain, I should withhold assent from those same opinions just as carefully as from what could be shown to be manifestly false.

11. But it is not enough to have made these observations. I must also take care to remember them. For those old, customary opinions keep coming back. Long and familiar use gives them the right to occupy my mind, even almost against my will, and to take control of my belief. I will not lose the habit of deferring to them and trusting them so long as I consider them what they truly are, namely, opinions that are to some extent doubtful, as I have already shown, but still highly probable, and that it is much more reasonable to believe than to deny. For this reason I am persuaded that I will not be doing wrong if, deliberately taking the opposite judgment, I become my own deceiver. I will suppose for a time that all those opinions are entirely false and imaginary, until at length I have balanced my old prejudices against my new ones, and my judgment is no longer turned aside by distorted habit from the path that may lead to the perception of truth. For I am assured that in the meantime this course will bring neither danger nor error, and that I cannot for now yield too much to distrust, since the end I am seeking is not action but knowledge.

note: Kept formula how often? As often as I think was changed to for how long.
replacement: 6. But [as for myself, what can I now say that I am], since I suppose there is an extremely powerful and, if I may say so, malignant being whose whole effort is directed to deceiving me? Can I affirm that I have any one of the attributes I have just described as belonging to the nature of body? I consider them attentively in my own mind, and I find none of them that can properly be said to belong to me. To list them would be idle and tedious. Let us pass, then, to the attributes of the soul. The first named were nutrition and walking. But if it is true that I have no body, it is also true that I can neither walk nor be nourished. Perception is another attribute of the soul. But perception too is impossible without the body. Besides, I have often believed in sleep that I perceived things which I afterward saw I had not really perceived. Thinking is another attribute of the soul, and here I find what properly belongs to me. This alone cannot be separated from me. I am — I exist: this is certain. But how often? As often as I think. For perhaps it could even happen, if I wholly ceased to think, that I would at the same time wholly cease to be. I now admit nothing that is not necessarily true. Precisely speaking, then, I am only a thinking thing, that is, a mind (mens sive animus), understanding, or reason, terms whose meaning I did not know before. Yet I am a real thing, and really exist. But what thing? I have answered: a thinking thing.

note: Purpose clause turned into a prediction and I know not what dropped.
replacement: 10. From this I begin to know what I am a little more clearly and distinctly than before. But it still seems to me, and I cannot help believing, that corporeal things, whose images are formed by thought [which fall under the senses] and are examined by thought, are known much more distinctly than that part of myself, I know not what, which cannot be imagined. It may indeed seem strange to say that I know and comprehend more distinctly things whose existence appears doubtful to me, which are unknown and do not belong to me, than things of whose reality I am persuaded, which are known to me and belong to my own nature. In a word, it seems strange to say that I know them more distinctly than I know myself. But I see clearly what is happening. My mind likes to wander, and will not yet submit to being held within the limits of truth. Let us therefore leave the mind to itself once more, and give it every kind of liberty [to consider the objects that appear to it from outside], so that, having drawn it away from these gently and at the right moment [and fixed it on the consideration of its being and the properties it finds in itself], it may then be more easily controlled.

note: From these appearances dropped from the judgment.
replacement: 13. Meanwhile, I am greatly astonished when I observe [the weakness of my mind and] how prone it is to error. For although I consider all this silently in my own mind, without giving any expression to what I think, words still sometimes get in my way, and I am almost led into error by the terms of ordinary language. We say, for example, that we see the same wax when it is before us, and not that we judge it to be the same because it keeps the same color and figure. From this I would immediately be inclined to conclude that the wax is known by the act of sight and not by the intuition of the mind alone, were it not for a similar case: human beings passing in the street below, as seen from a window. In this case I do not hesitate to say that I see the men themselves, just as I say that I see the wax. Yet what do I see from the window besides hats and cloaks, which might cover artificial machines moved by springs? But from these appearances I judge that they are human beings. And so I comprehend, by the faculty of judgment alone which is in my mind, what I believed I saw with my eyes.
